questions.q: What is the correct chronological order of the following language milestones: (a) telegraphic speech, (b) babbling, (c) holophrastic stage, (d) cooing?
questions.a: Correct order: cooing (1-3 months) → babbling (4-6 months) → holophrastic stage (10-18 months) → telegraphic speech (24-30 months). A wrong answer (e.g., placing telegraphic before holophrastic) reveals the student thinks grammar emerges before single-word symbols, confusing syntactic complexity with lexical acquisition.

questions.q: A 20-month-old says "ball" while pointing at a ball, and later says "ball" while reaching for a ball on a high shelf. In the first case the word labels an object; in the second it expresses a request. What does this illustrate about the holophrastic stage?
questions.a: It illustrates that a single holophrase can carry multiple pragmatic functions (naming, requesting, protesting) because the child lacks syntactic markers like imperatives or interrogatives. A wrong answer (e.g., "the child knows two different words") shows the student conflates word form with communicative intent, missing the core concept of holophrasis.

questions.q: A 28-month-old says "Daddy go work" and "Me want cookie." Identify the stage and list two grammatical morphemes that are systematically omitted in this stage.
questions.a: Stage: telegraphic speech. Omitted morphemes: auxiliary verb "is" (in "Daddy go work") and pronoun case/subject "I" (in "Me want cookie"). A wrong answer (e.g., "past tense -ed") reveals the student does not distinguish between content words (retained) and function words (omitted) in telegraphic speech.

questions.q: Compare the cognitive demands of the two-word stage versus the telegraphic stage. Why does the telegraphic stage require advances in both working memory and syntactic rule extraction?
questions.a: Two-word stage only requires combining two semantic units (e.g., "more milk") without internal grammar. Telegraphic stage requires ordering three or more words according to language-specific rules (e.g., SVO in English) while holding the utterance plan in working memory. A wrong answer (e.g., "telegraphic is just longer") misses the shift from associative pairing to rule-governed syntax.

questions.q: Critique the claim: "Babbling is meaningless motor practice; it has no linguistic significance." Use evidence from cross-linguistic babbling studies and the transition to first words.
questions.a: The claim is false. Babbling shows language-specific phonetic patterns (e.g., French babies babble with more nasal vowels), and the consonant-vowel sequences in late babbling (canonical babbling) directly scaffold the phonological forms of first words. A wrong answer (e.g., "babbling is just exercise") ignores the continuity between pre-linguistic and linguistic phonology.

questions.q: Design a 5-minute observation checklist for a 30-month-old that would allow you to confirm the child has entered the early complex-sentence stage. Include at least three specific syntactic structures to listen for.
questions.a: Checklist: (1) Coordination with "and" (e.g., "I play and eat"), (2) Subordination with "because" or "if" (e.g., "I cry because fall"), (3) Wh-questions with auxiliary inversion (e.g., "Where did Daddy go?"), (4) Negation with auxiliary "not" (e.g., "I not sleep"). A poor answer (e.g., "listens for longer sentences") fails to specify the grammatical markers that distinguish complex syntax from long telegraphic strings.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Language development is the universal, biologically guided process through which infants progress from reflexive ______ to fully grammatical speech, passing through invariant stages: cooing (1-3 months), babbling (4-6 months), holophrastic one-word utterances (10-18 months), two-word combinations (18-24 months), telegraphic speech (24-30 months), and increasingly complex syntactic structures (30+ months), each stage building on the maturation of Broca's and Wernicke's areas and interaction with a linguistic environment.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are watching a home video of your baby cousin: at 2 months she coos "ooo-aaa" when smiled at; at 6 months she babbles "bababa"; at 14 months she points at a dog and says "doggy!"; at 22 months she demands "more milk"; at 30 months she declares "Mommy go store"; and at 4 years she asks "Why did the cat hide under the bed?" Notice how each clip adds a new layer — vowels, consonants, single symbols, word ______, grammar, and complex clauses.
What is Language development? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Language development is the universal, biologically guided process through which infants progress from reflexive vocalizations to fully grammatical speech, passing through invariant stages: cooing (1-3 months), babbling (4-6 months), holophrastic one-word utterances (10-18 months), two-word combinations (18-24 months), telegraphic speech.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Language development?
questions.a: Students often believe that "telegraphic speech" means the child speaks in short, incomplete sentences because of low intelligence or lack of exposure.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) sequence the six major stages of language development with approximate age ranges and hallmark features, and (2) analyze a brief transcript of child speech to identify the stage and explain which grammatical morphemes or syntactic rules are present or absent.
